Row 140 (n=314): "meeting with Ana, note: bring the contract"
sop: c1 nonfinite verb="meeting"; r1 with c1→n1(Ana); c2 imperative verb="note"; c3 imperative bring complement n2(the contract); r2 from c2 to c1; k1 c2 c3.
Fault: "meeting" as verb of a nonfinite clause — noun made verb → L1 (as n=278/291/297). Though here "meeting" could be a participle?? "meeting with Ana, note: bring the contract" — "meeting" is a noun (a meeting event). So L1.

Correction:

@r1 syntax.relation marker="with" from=$n1 to=$n2
@n2 syntax.nominal head="Ana"

@c2 syntax.clause form=nonfinite verb="bring" complement=$n4
@n4 syntax.nominal dependent="the" head="contract"
@r3 syntax.relation from=$n3 to=$c2

Hmm, "note: bring the contract" — content. Keep "note" as a nominal tied to the fragment clause, and the content clause tied to "note" as nonfinite. Good. But should the content be a clause with verb "bring" (nonfinite) — yes.

Row 141 (n=315): "call with Lee tomorrow - agenda: pricing"
sop: c1 form=imperative verb="call" modifier=tomorrow; r1 with c1→n1(Lee); n2 agenda; n3 pricing; r2 from c2 to c1; c2 fragment complement n2; r3 n2→n3.
Fault: "call" as imperative verb — "call with Lee tomorrow" is not a command; it's a noun phrase ("call" = meeting). Hmm! "call" can be a verb, but here "call with Lee" is a noun. Per the settled case: "A command needs its verb. When the first word of a message with no other verb can be a noun or a verb ('book design review', 'schedule the kickoff'), it is the verb; held as a noun in a fragment, the command is lost: L1." The reverse: is holding "call" as a verb wrong here? The message "call with Lee tomorrow - agenda: pricing" — no other verb. If "call" is a verb, the message is a command "call with Lee tomorrow" — but "call with Lee" as a command is ungrammatical ("call with" is not a verb+preposition phrase for phoning Lee... actually "call with Lee" could mean "call [someone] with Lee"?). Hmm, we can't use world knowledge. 

The trap in the settled case is one-directional: a command must not lose its verb. Here the circuit reads the message as a command. Is that a wrong statement? "call with Lee tomorrow" as a command — a reader could go "call [me] with Lee tomorrow"? Reads oddly. But grammar: "call" as a verb, "with Lee" as a relation, "tomorrow" modifier. Hmm, plausible enough? The message has "agenda: pricing" as a separate label. Since "call" can be a verb and the words don't settle it ("A word that grammar allows as a noun or as a verb" — several readings pass), I'd accept L8 under that rule.

Hmm, but the settled case says when the first word can be a noun or verb, it must be the verb (else L1). That's when it's a command. Here the reading "call" = verb gives a command; the reading "call" = noun gives a fragment. The formalizer chose verb → allowed by the "word that grammar allows as noun or verb" leniency. Accept L8.

Row 142 (n=317): "Retro Friday, notes: what went wrong with the release"
sop: n1 Retro; n2 Friday; n3 notes; n4 what; c1 form=interrogative verb=went modifier=wrong subject=n4(what); r1 with c1→n5(the release); c2 fragment complement n1, n2, n3; k1 conjunct c2 c1.
Fault: "what went wrong with the release" — a clause opening with a question word inside another clause (the content of the notes) → per settled case, its form is declarative; written interrogative = L1. Also "what" as the subject — hmm, "what went wrong": "what" is the subject of "went" ✓ (that's how grammar puts it: "the head of a nominal in 'what is this?'" — here n4 head "what" with subject role ✓).
So L1 for the interrogative. Quote: 'what went wrong with the release'.
